'''Qatabānian''' (or '''Qatabānic'''),<ref name="Multitree"/> one of the four better-documented languages of the [[Old South Arabian]] (or "Ṣayhadic") sub-group of South [[Semitic languages|Semitic]], was spoken mainly but not exclusively in the kingdom of [[Qataban|Qatabān]], located in central Yemen. The language is attested between 500 BC and 200 AD. Some two thousand inscriptions are known and written in the [[Old South Arabian alphabet|Ancient South Arabian Monumental Script]], known as ''Musnad''. These inscriptions are mainly found in Wādī Bayhān and Wādī Ḥārib to the south-east of Ma'rib, and from the plateau to the south of that area. Qatabanian inscriptions increase after the beginning of the 4th century BC when the [[Sabaeans]] ceased to dominate the area, and Qatabān became an independent kingdom.

Qatabanian was spoken in an area across the kingdom of Qatabān as far as [[Jabal al-'Awd]] (near [[Zafar, Yemen|Zafar]]) in the southwest, and if we are to believe the Greek and Latin writers, it went as far as [[Bab al-Mandab|Bāb al-Mandab]] on the Red Sea. At the end of the 2nd century AD, [[Saba']] and [[Hadramawt|Ḥaḑramawt]] finally defeated Qatabān, and the inscriptions ended.<ref>{{cite book|first1=Leonid |last1=Kogan |first2=Andrey |last2=Korotayev |author-link2=Andrey Korotayev |chapter=Ṣayhadic Languages (Epigraphic South Arabian |title=Semitic Languages |location=London |publisher=[[Routledge]] |date=1997 |pages=157–183}}</ref>

The language used to write inscriptions in the kingdom of [[Kingdom of Awsan|Awsān]], known as Awsānian (or Awsānite), is virtually identical to Qatabānic, but it is so poorly attested (25 inscriptions) that it remains uncertain whether it is a Qatabānic dialect or a distinct language.

== Numerals ==
Qatabānian has an unusual form for the [[cardinal number]] "one": ''ṭd'' / fem. ''ṭt''; this has no known cognates in any of the ancient Semitic languages, although it does appear in modern South Arabian languages (cf. [[Shehri language|Jibbālī]] ''ṭad'', fem. ''ṭit''). Qatabānian also has another word for "one", ''ˤs<sub>1</sub>tn'', which is cognate with the [[Minaean]] ''ˤs<sub>1</sub>t''{{sfn|Nebes|Stein|2004|p=472}} (and with forms in [[Akkadian language|Akkadian]], [[Ugaritic]] and [[Hebrew]]).<ref>{{cite journal|first=Giovanni |last=Mazzini |title=Some Qatabanian Lexical Items |journal=Aula Orientalis |volume=29 |date=2011 |pages=121–129}}</ref> The Qatabānian forms for "three" and "six" are the same as the Old Sabaean words: ''s<sub>2</sub>lṯ'' (fem. ''s<sub>2</sub>lṯt'') and ''s<sub>1</sub>dṯ'' (fem. ''s<sub>1</sub>dṯt'').

Qatabānian expresses distributives by repeating the number, thus: b-ˤs<sub>2</sub>r ˤs<sub>2</sub>r ḫbṣtm mṣˤm l-ṭt ṭt ywmm "ten full Ḫabṣat coins each for each day".{{sfn|Nebes|Stein|2004|p=472}}
